Adi Leon, son of Nurit and Amir, was born on 20 Adar I 5763 (22 February 2003) in the community of Nili, in the Mateh Binyamin Regional Council. He is the brother of Zohar and Uri. Adi grew up and was educated in Nili, attended the local elementary school until eighth grade, and then attended Ironi Hey High School and the "Me'ouf Branko Weiss" High School in the city of Modiin-Maccabim-Re'ut. From a young age he stood out for his wisdom, his joy in life, and the constant smile that lit up his face. A natural leader, he was always at the center of his group, and all his friends gravitated to him. He knew how to unite and bond everyone, giving a place to each person. He connected easily with anyone and formed deep, long-lasting friendships with people from all over the country, of every age and lifestyle.

After school hours, he was a member of the youth movement Maccabi Tzair, and later became an instructor and part of the adult staff of the Nili branch. Until he was drafted into the army, he led the young people of the community and instilled in his members a love of the land, which was an inseparable part of him. Above all, he loved music, and already as a child he showed talent in the field and saw it as his future. At the age of thirteen he opened a gardening business with a good friend, and with the money they earned they bought sound equipment and began producing events and parties together. Later, his parents built him a studio in the backyard, where he created electronic music. Adi left behind two music channels, on YouTube and SoundCloud, under the name Leon: https://youtube.com/@Leon-cs8oo?si=m0QnZRB646qrceAh https://soundcloud.app.goo.gl/r2pu17C51BNyPWWJA

Before his enlistment, he made clear that he intended to serve in a combat unit, although he also received an invitation to tryouts for a cyber unit. He enlisted in the IDF on 16 August 2021 and served as a fighter in the "Tzabar" battalion of the Givati Brigade, after successfully completing basic training. From the start he was slated for command and was assigned to the command squad of his platoon. Two weeks before the Maches HaKoma (the final march of the Giv'ati training) he was injured and diagnosed with a torn knee ligament. Nevertheless, he insisted on taking part in the march, although he was not medically fit for it, and walked the march with his comrades. Afterward he explained to his parents that there was no chance he would receive the purple beret without completing the march. Because of his injury and lack of medical fitness, he did not attend the squad commanders' course. After a waiting period in the battalion, and in light of his abilities, he was assigned to the instructional staff of the August 2022 recruit platoon as the platoon's deputy commander for the company's second squad. After accompanying his recruits through the eight months of training, he insisted on returning to the battalion as a fighter. He was happy in the battalion and later told his parents that it was the best decision he had made. He felt that his calling was to be a fighter.

Adi was a professional soldier, full of motivation, with a sense of mission and pride, and he loved the land and the homeland with all his heart. His motto was "Smile!" and he lived by it: he made the most of every moment, spread joy wherever he went, and lifted the spirits of everyone he met. Adi always helped willingly, even when no one had asked him to, and he knew how to make everyone around him feel good. He had friends from every corner of society and a special ability to strengthen those who struggled and make them part of the group. One of his fellow soldiers, a yeshiva student, recounted that when they served in a barren desert area he asked Adi to try to arrange an eruv chatzerot for him before Shabbat (a cord stretched around an inhabited area to permit actions otherwise forbidden on Shabbat, such as carrying from one domain to another). Adi, who came from a secular home, had never heard of an eruv before. He questioned his friend about what it was and what was done with the cord, and once he understood its meaning, he did everything he could to help. They were in the heart of the desert with almost nothing around them, but Adi did not give up. He turned over stone after stone until he found a suitable cord, tied it around the position, and made a thoroughly proper eruv. For his friend it was an entire world, and for Adi, mutual help came naturally, even when it related to worlds he did not know.

Adi had many dreams and a bright future ahead of him. In mid-April 2024 he was due to finish his army service, and he planned to travel, play music, and share his works around the world.

On Shabbat, 22 Tishrei 5784, Simchat Torah, 7 October 2023, at 6:30 in the morning, the Hamas terror organization launched a surprise attack on Israel. Under cover of massive barrages of missiles and rockets from the Gaza Strip into wide areas of the country, thousands of terrorists infiltrated by land, sea, and air, and began a murderous assault on the communities of the Gaza envelope, on Sderot, Ofakim and Netivot, on the trance party site near the Re'im and Nir Oz kibbutzim, on IDF bases, and on travelers on the roads in the area. The terrorists murdered some 800 civilians in their homes and in their cars, after committing grave atrocities against them. They abducted hundreds of Israelis to the Gaza Strip and destroyed, looted, and set fire to homes and property. Hundreds of soldiers, police officers, security personnel, and members of local emergency squads fell in battle. That morning, a war began.

Adi was at home on a regular leave and had returned that morning from a party where he had spent the whole night. At around 9:00, after a night without any sleep at all, he was called back to the battalion, which was at that time training in the Golan Heights. After gearing up, he entered with his battalion comrades into fierce fighting in Kfar Aza kibbutz. He fought bravely against the many terrorists who were still in the kibbutz and helped rescue local residents. After three days of fighting in the kibbutz, he called his parents and told them that he "had seen things that no one in life should have to see..."

In the three weeks that followed, the battalion moved into a period of training and preparation for the ground incursion. During this time he managed to meet his parents three times at the training grounds. During one of these meetings, his parents told him that he and his comrades were standing at a historic crossroads for the State of Israel, and that in twenty years he would be able to tell his children how, thanks to them, we are living here.

On 27 October, the first infantry forces entered the fighting. Adi fought in the vanguard platoon that led the battalion in the first armored personnel carriers into the Strip. After four days of intense fighting, during a battle in northern Gaza, an anti-tank missile struck the armored personnel carrier in which he was serving with eleven other soldiers. Ten of the soldiers were killed on the spot. Adi and one other soldier were wounded and evacuated, first to an evacuation APC and then by helicopter to Ichilov Hospital. But there, shortly after his arrival, he was pronounced dead due to severe internal injuries. His evacuation by helicopter of Unit 669 was documented in Air Force Magazine, issue no. 274, February 2024, in an article titled "Adi's Last Flight."

Staff Sergeant First Class Adi Leon fell in battle on 16 Cheshvan 5784 (31 October 2023), at the age of twenty. He was laid to rest in the military section of the cemetery in Modiin. He is survived by his parents and two sisters. On his tombstone the family inscribed the words: "Adidush, with the eternal smile and the music in his heart."

During the shiva, his parents were given a notebook he had written before entering the Gaza Strip, containing farewell letters to his parents, each of his sisters, his extended family, his friends, and the State. On its cover he wrote: "To be read after my death," identifying himself as "Adi Leon, Tzabar, Givati, rifleman, point." To his parents he wrote: "I never thought I would have to write something like this in my life. I tried to put it off and put it off, but we were told that tomorrow we are going into Gaza and there is a chance we won't come back. And there are a few things I must tell you before this is over. Dear Mom and Dad, although I don't show you much love and don't give you much of my time, know that I appreciate you so much. Even when I went through a hard time you never stopped trying to get close and help. Even though I spoke to you disrespectfully and gave up on everything, you never gave up on me. You always made sure we had everything and never lacked anything, and you work very hard for it. You raised us in an amazing way, and I began to see it most clearly when Zohar grew up. Recently I was hardly ever home, and even when I was, I wasn't really there. I am so sorry that I didn't devote more time to the family and only looked for ways to have fun. In the end, family is everything, and you always accepted me as I am. You are my entire world."

To his sister Zohar he wrote: "Zohar, my amazing sister. I am writing this and remembering all our moments together as children, how we enjoyed ourselves and never stopped looking for mischief, from getting up before our parents in the morning to make them breakfast, to filming funny videos together and pretending we were famous, how we drove Uri crazy endlessly and couldn't stop laughing until our stomachs hurt. Now we've grown up and each of us is busy with our own life, you in your room and me at parties. I miss our childhood together so much. Now you are the eldest sister. It's a hard task, but I'm sure you'll manage, because that's who you are: responsible, smart, caring. Some would say 'the successful sister.' I love you so much, and it's important to me that you remember this. It's a shame I can't say it to you face to face."

To his sister Uri he wrote: "Ourika, my little sister, I don't think God could create anything as cute and perfect as you. I'm writing this after two weeks without seeing you, and it feels like an eternity. I wish I could hug you one last time. You are only ten and still so innocent. I always enjoy seeing you excited and moved and discovering new things. It reminds me of myself. Sometimes I even envy you. I don't know how a girl your age is supposed to read something like this or how you'll take it, but always remember that I love you and miss you. And if you want, you can talk to me in your thoughts, and I'll listen to you from above too."

To his extended family he wrote: "I can't write to everyone, because I really got to know a lot of people during my life, but still, I want to thank you for all the moments and experiences you gave me. The Leon family and the Perlberg family, I always felt comfortable with you: the warm, homey atmosphere, the giving, the humor. I always had a sense that there was a bit of each one of you in me. Thank you for everything. I truly love you, and I'm sorry for every family meal or event I missed, because I know I missed amazing experiences and amazing people."

To his close friends, both boys and girls, he wrote: "To my good friends, we really have so many experiences together that I can't even begin to list them. Thank you for always being there for me and for building me an amazing childhood. I hope you'll celebrate as we planned when I come back, and that you'll tell your children about all the moments and experiences I shared with you. I miss you."

He ended with a letter to the State, in which he wrote: "I am going into this war knowing I may not come back, but I believe with my whole heart in what I am doing. We have no other land, and now it is my turn to defend it and to avenge all the civilians and soldiers, the babies, the elderly, and all the women who were simply helpless in the face of Hamas's inferno. This is the education my parents gave me. This is what I believe in. I hope you will remember me. Adi."

His sister Zohar wrote on her birthday, after his death: "For as long as I can remember, I would get a message from Adi at midnight saying 'Happy birthday, sister.' No matter how far apart we were, he never forgot... Thank you for an amazing childhood, for always being there for me, for never letting me feel alone, and for strengthening me in hard moments as well as good ones. Thank you for the experiences, the laughter, and the special bond that was only mine and yours, because with you it was undoubtedly true love."

His relatives wrote: "Adi managed everything, or more precisely, almost everything. Adi was at every possible party, went out every day and every night. Adi built himself the studio of his dreams, and while everyone else studied at school, he would sit and create music. Adi danced, was happy, laughed, and smiled at every possible moment. He did everything not quite by the book. He understood that life is limited, and he used it in the best way possible."

Adi's final letter became a source of inspiration for many and a significant part of his commemoration. Excerpts from the letter were quoted at the State Memorial Day ceremony held on 4 Iyar 5784 (12 May 2024) on Mount Herzl in Jerusalem, and at many official memorial ceremonies across the country. The President of the State chose to read excerpts from his letter on several occasions, and it has been mentioned countless times at various events. The annual music show of the "Me'ouf Branko Weiss" High School, the "Festibranko 2024," was dedicated to Adi's memory, and within it the song "Always in the Heart" was written and composed, inspired by the letter he left behind. All the linking segments of the show were also taken from music he created. The musician Yoav Asif also created a song inspired by the letter, titled "Now It's My Turn." The musician Omer Koren, who composed the melody for Haim Gouri's song "Made of Letters," dedicated that song to Adi, and throughout the music video accompanying it, the full words of the letter he left behind appear on screen. All three songs can be heard on YouTube.

From Adi's final letter an educational values kit was created called "Adi's Lights," dealing with eight values reflected in the words he wrote. The kit is distributed in Israel and abroad, in many languages, in a range of settings including the Ministry of Education, pre-military preparatory programs, the IDF, youth movements, and many communities around the world. The kit makes it possible to connect with these values through the figure of a special young Israeli who fell defending the country. It is distributed in print and digitally through an association established under the name "Adi's Lights – In Memory of Staff Sergeant Adi Leon z"l." Link to "Adi's Lights": https://lp.vp4.me/t15y Link to "Adi's Lights" in various languages: https://lp.smoove.io/twct#zHeader

Adi's handwriting was turned into a font as part of the "Ot.Hayim" project and was selected to serve as the text font on the cover of the album by the musician Chen Porati. In Nili, where he grew up, the main street is named after him: "Ma'ale Adi Leon." In the city of Modiin-Maccabim-Re'ut, where he was educated and spent many hours of his youth, a street in the city center, between Ficus and Levonah Streets, is named after him. At the Nili elementary school he attended, a large mosaic wall was erected in which Adi is commemorated, and at the Nili branch of the youth movement Maccabi Tzair a study corner was established in his memory. A memorial page was opened in his name on Instagram under remember_adi_leon, on Facebook under the same name, and on TikTok under adileonforeveryoung. The music Adi created can be heard on YouTube and SoundCloud under the artist name Leon.

Adi is commemorated in many other initiatives. He is part of a book, distributed under the title "If You Read These Words," which gathers letters of fallen soldiers; according to its authors, Adi's letter was the inspiration for it. A drawing of the cat he left for his younger sister, and the final words of his letter, "...I hope you will remember me...," have been included in it. Several articles have been written about him, in Israel and abroad, and the story of his life is commemorated in various writing projects. Adi, his family wrote, asked at the end of his letter "...I hope you will remember me..." and signed with a heart and a Star of David, and the family works to fulfill this request.
